e.t: This word means “to take up.” It describes the action of lifting or taking something up, and it functions as a verb in the Greek New Testament. Its ordinary sense can apply to physically taking something, gathering it, or carrying it away, depending on the sentence. The word occurs 101 times in the Greek New Testament, so its precise force in any particular verse comes from the surrounding context.

e.t: This word means “truly,” expressing that something is real, certain, or genuinely so. It is used as an adverb, adding assurance to a statement rather than naming a person, object, or action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 18 times across 18 verses. Its repeated use shows a steady function: it strengthens the truth or reliability of what is being said. The surrounding words determine exactly what claim it emphasizes in each verse, but its central sense remains a firm affirmation of truth.

This Greek New Testament word means “refreshment.” It refers to relief or renewal that restores someone’s strength and well-being. As a noun, it names the experience or provision of being refreshed rather than describing an action. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 3:20. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains refreshment: a restorative benefit received by a person.

This word refers to an enemy or opponent—a person who stands against someone in conflict or opposition. It is used five times in the Greek New Testament, across four verses, and can describe an adversary in an ordinary dispute or a hostile spiritual enemy. Its central idea is not merely difference or disagreement, but active opposition between parties. The surrounding verse determines whether the opponent is human or portrayed as a spiritual adversary.

e.t: This word describes the act of hanging or strangling someone. Its central meaning is physical death caused by suspending or constricting a person, expressed by the glosses “to hang” and “to strangle.” It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at Matthew 27:5. The word’s precise force in that passage belongs to the surrounding verse and context, but its basic lexical sense concerns the act itself rather than a person, place, or abstract idea.

This word means “answer”: a spoken response given to a question, statement, or challenge. It describes the reply itself rather than the subject being discussed. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, all in Luke and John, where its basic sense remains a response offered in conversation. The surrounding words determine whether the answer is brief, explanatory, or defensive, but the word itself identifies the act or content of replying. Its normal meaning is therefore a direct answer given to someone who has spoken.

Aristarchus is a personal name, referring to a man rather than expressing a general idea or action. In the Greek New Testament, the name identifies one individual who appears five times: three times in Acts, and once each in Colossians and Philemon. The repeated rendering “Aristarchus” indicates that the name is retained rather than translated into an ordinary descriptive word. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself tells us who is being identified, while each passage supplies the details about his role and circumstances.

This word refers to food as something consumed, or to the act of eating. It presents nourishment in a plain, concrete sense rather than naming a particular dish or meal. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 11 times in 10 verses, including passages that contrast ordinary food with what has lasting value and passages that mention eating directly. Its exact force in a sentence depends on whether the context emphasizes the food itself or the act of consuming it.

e.t: This word means “to break in,” referring to entering by forcing through a barrier rather than entering normally. It is a verb describing an act of unlawful or unexpected entry. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, appearing in passages that use the possibility of a thief breaking into a house as an illustration. The basic idea remains physical intrusion: someone gains entry by breaking through or opening a way into a secured place. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

e.t: This word means “seventy,” the number that comes after sixty-nine and before seventy-one. It is used in the Greek New Testament as a numerical term, identifying a count or quantity rather than describing a person, action, or spiritual quality. The word occurs five times in the Greek New Testament, in Luke and Acts. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the people or things being counted there, but its basic meaning remains the number seventy.

e.t: This word means “be active” or “to be at work in.” It describes something operating, producing an effect, or actively working within a person or situation. It can refer to forces at work, suffering that produces a result, or God’s activity expressed through people. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 21 times, so it has a broad use while retaining the central idea of active operation. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what or whom the word describes.

e.t: This word means “to reach out to” or “to strain toward.” It describes actively extending oneself forward toward something ahead, rather than remaining focused on what is behind. As a verb, it expresses purposeful effort and forward movement. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Philippians 3:13. Its exact force in that verse is understood from the surrounding passage, but the word itself presents the picture of stretching forward with focused intent.

This word means “rivalry” or “selfish ambition”—a determined pursuit of one’s own interests in competition with others. It describes contentious striving rather than humble cooperation, and Scripture places it among attitudes that produce conflict and division. The word occurs seven times in the Greek New Testament, including passages that warn against it and contrast it with humility and peace. Its central idea is self-seeking competition that sets personal advancement against the good of others.

This word means “gladly” or “most gladly.” It is an adverb describing an action done with willing pleasure, showing that someone embraces or welcomes what he is doing rather than doing it reluctantly. The stronger rendering “most gladly” can express especially willing or joyful acceptance. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both in 2 Corinthians 12. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is clear: acting with glad willingness.

Elijah is a personal name referring to the biblical figure known by that name. In the Greek New Testament, it appears 29 times, consistently identifying Elijah rather than describing a general quality, action, or object. The name occurs in discussions of his appearance, identity, and expected connection with events spoken of by Jesus and others. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is simply the name Elijah.

This word means “hair” or “hairs,” referring to the strands growing from a person’s body. It can describe hair generally or individual hairs, depending on the sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 15 times across 14 verses, showing ordinary use for something small and countable as well as hair considered collectively. Its meaning remains straightforward: the visible strands themselves, rather than a figurative idea supplied by the word alone.

This word means “priest” or “priests,” naming a person or group identified by that title. It functions as a noun and can refer to one priest or more than one. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 31 times across 31 verses, including references in Matthew, Luke, John, Hebrews, and Revelation. The word’s basic meaning remains the same whether it appears in the singular or plural form.

Jerusalem is the name of the important city in the New Testament. It functions as a place-name, referring to a specific city rather than describing an action or quality. The city is mentioned 62 times in the Greek New Testament, appearing from Matthew through Galatians. References to Jerusalem occur in accounts involving Jesus’ ministry, his final approach, his death, and the early Christian community, but the word itself consistently identifies the city. Its meaning is simply “Jerusalem.”

Joses is a personal name, rendered as “Joses.” It identifies people mentioned in the Greek New Testament rather than describing a quality, action, or object. This name occurs three times, all in Mark: Mark 6:3, Mark 15:40, and Mark 15:47. Without the surrounding verse text, the name alone does not establish whether these references concern the same person or different people. Its basic lexical meaning is therefore simply the proper name Joses.

This word refers to a court or a lawsuit—the legal setting or proceeding in which a dispute is judged. It can describe a court of law rather than the people involved in judging. In the Greek New Testament, it appears three times, in 1 Corinthians and James. Its exact sense may be either the court itself or the legal case, depending on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is formal legal judgment or litigation.

The word means “grandmother,” referring to a person’s mother’s or father’s mother. It identifies a family relationship and a female ancestor one generation above a parent. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Timothy 1:5. The word itself names this family relation; understanding its particular significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and its description of the person mentioned there.

This word means “change of mind” or “repentance.” It names a real turning in a person’s outlook: the person no longer remains settled in the former way, but changes direction inwardly. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 22 times and is consistently rendered “repentance,” showing that this is a recurring biblical term rather than a rare expression. Its precise force in any verse is understood from the surrounding passage, but its central idea is a changed mind expressed as repentance.

This word refers to a “teacher of the law”—someone identified by teaching the law. It describes a recognized teaching role rather than the law itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, appearing in Luke, Acts, and 1 Timothy. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning consistently points to a person whose role involves instructing others in the law.

This word means “donkey,” the ordinary term for that animal. In the Greek New Testament, it refers to a donkey as a real animal used in everyday settings, including transportation and riding. The word occurs five times, all in five verses: three times in Matthew, once in Luke, and once in John. Its use in these passages remains straightforward and concrete; the word itself identifies the animal rather than expressing a separate abstract quality or action. The surrounding verse determines what the donkey is doing or why it is mentioned.

e.t: This word means “to form a mob” or “to riot.” It describes the act of gathering people into a disorderly crowd, especially for disruptive or hostile action. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 17:5. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning centers on creating a mob or engaging in a riot rather than simply gathering peacefully.

e.t: This word means “to defect” or “to fall away.” It describes a person turning aside from a position, commitment, or former attachment rather than remaining loyal to it. It is a verb, expressing the act of abandoning or departing. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Hebrews 6:6. The surrounding passage is needed to understand precisely how this act is being described there, but the word itself centers on defection or falling away from what one previously held.

This word refers to acquiring something or to what is possessed. It can describe the obtaining of something, or a possession held as one’s own. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, including passages that speak of a promised possession and of a people belonging to God. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on receiving or holding. Its central idea is secure acquisition or ownership rather than a passing experience.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to provoke.” It describes an action that prompts or incites a response from another person. The word appears once in the Greek New Testament, in Galatians 5:26. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, this entry states the word’s normal lexical meaning rather than explaining the specific situation in that verse. The exact force of the provocation depends on its context.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb expresses the action of planning something or presenting it. Its listed meanings include “I planned,” “presented,” “to plan,” “to plan/present,” and “to present,” so its exact English wording depends on how it functions in the sentence. It occurs three times in the Greek New Testament: twice in Romans and once in Ephesians. The word therefore concerns either setting something forward intentionally or bringing it forward for others to see, with the surrounding verse determining which sense is intended.

The word refers to a winnowing fork, a farm tool used in handling harvested grain. It names an object rather than an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Matthew 3:12 and Luke 3:17. Those references show its limited New Testament usage, while the precise force of the image in either passage belongs to the surrounding verse and passage context.

“Hardness of heart” describes an inner condition that is resistant, unresponsive, or unwilling to receive what is true and right. It portrays the heart as firm rather than receptive, affecting a person’s response to God and his commands. This expression appears three times in the Greek New Testament, in Matthew and Mark. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains an inward refusal to soften or respond rightly.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to preserve” or “to protect.” It describes keeping something safe, retaining it carefully, or guarding it from loss. The word appears three times in the Greek New Testament, so its basic sense is consistent while the surrounding passage determines what is being preserved or protected. Syracuse is a proper name referring to the place called Syracuse. In the Greek New Testament, this name appears once, in Acts 28:12, and it is rendered “Syracuse.” Because it is a place name rather than a term describing an action, quality, or teaching, its basic meaning is simply the identification of that location. The surrounding verse supplies the particular role Syracuse has in the account, while the name itself identifies the place.

This word means “clear proof” or “convincing proof”—something that provides firm confirmation rather than a weak indication. It describes evidence intended to establish that a matter is true and reliable. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 1:3. The word’s central idea is the certainty produced by proof that can persuade or assure those who receive it. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the specific matter being confirmed.

This word means “insult” or “mistreatment”—harmful treatment that dishonors, abuses, or wrongs another person. It describes more than simple inconvenience; it points to degrading or injurious treatment directed toward someone. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, in Acts and 2 Corinthians. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains the experience or act of being treated abusively or contemptuously.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to receive” or “to welcome.” It describes accepting someone, taking them in, or giving them a place of reception. The word appears four times in the New Testament, in Luke, Acts, and James, showing a normal action of receiving people rather than an abstract idea. Its exact emphasis—whether simple acceptance, hospitality, or welcoming someone into one’s home—depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

“Highest” describes what stands above all others in elevation, position, or rank. It points to the supreme place rather than merely something that is high. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs 13 times, including passages where “Highest” is used as a title referring to God. Its normal force is therefore comparative and superlative: it identifies the one or thing raised above every other. The surrounding verse determines precisely what is being described.

e.t: This word expresses that something “it should” happen or “it should be” so. It points to what is fitting, necessary, or expected rather than merely describing what happens. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in James 3:10, and functions as a brief statement about what ought to be. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning is the idea of obligation or proper expectation.

This word describes something that is falsely called or falsely identified—given a name or description that does not truly belong to it. It points to a misleading designation rather than merely an incorrect statement. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Timothy 6:20. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea is a name or claim presented as genuine when it is not.
